title: Ordinal Numbers for Grade 1: First, Second, Third to Tenth + Free Quiz
meta_title: Ordinal Numbers for Grade 1 (1st to 10th) + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Ordinal numbers for Grade 1 made simple: 1st to 10th, their spellings, and how position changes with where you start. Free quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: Cardinal numbers tell you how many; ordinal numbers tell you which one. Here is how I teach first, second and third to six-year-olds, why the answer flips when you count from the other end, and a quick quiz to check it stuck.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Line up five children for a photo and ask a Grade 1 class who is second. Half the room will point confidently — but at two different children, because half started counting from the left and half from the right. That little argument is the whole lesson in one moment. Ordinal numbers for Grade 1 are not really about learning new words; they are about agreeing on where you start.

An ordinal number tells you a position in an order — first, second, third, and so on. It is a different job from the numbers children already know. When we say ‘there are five apples’ we are counting how many; that is a cardinal number. When we say ‘take the third apple’ we are pointing at one spot in a line; that is an ordinal number. Same numbers, completely different question.

Cardinal versus ordinal: how many, or which one

This is the distinction I make sure lands before anything else, because everything after it depends on it. Cardinal answers ‘how many?’ Ordinal answers ‘which one in the line?’ A child can count to twenty perfectly and still freeze when you ask who came fourth in a race, because that is a genuinely different idea.

QuestionTypeExample answer
How many biscuits are there?CardinalSix biscuits
Which biscuit is Aarav eating?OrdinalThe second one
How many runners finished?CardinalEight runners
Where did Meera finish?OrdinalThird

The ordinals from first to tenth

For Grade 1, first to tenth is plenty. The words matter, and so does the short form we write next to a number — 1st, 2nd, 3rd — because children meet these on calendars, in queues and on quiz papers long before they can spell them.

NumberShort formWord
11stfirst
22ndsecond
33rdthird
44thfourth
55thfifth
66thsixth
77thseventh
88theighth
99thninth
1010thtenth

The three that trip children up

Most ordinals just add ‘th’ to the number, which is a comforting pattern for a six-year-old. The odd ones out are the first three — first, second, third — which sound nothing like one, two, three. I teach those three as their own little song and let the rest follow the ‘th’ rule. Watch for the sneaky spellings too: fifth (not fiveth), eighth (one ‘t’, said ‘ay-tth’), and ninth (the ‘e’ in nine disappears).

Position depends on where you start

Here is the idea that separates a child who has memorised the words from one who actually understands ordinals. Position is not fixed to a child — it depends on which end you count from. Take a row: Riya, Kabir, Sana, Dev, Priya, counting from the left.

  • From the left, Sana is third.
  • From the right, Sana is also third — but only because there are five in the row and she happens to sit in the middle.
  • Dev is fourth from the left, yet second from the right.
  • Riya is first from the left and fifth from the right — the same child, two different ordinals.

So the question is never just ‘which position is Dev?’ It is ‘which position is Dev, counting from which end?’ In my experience teaching six-year-olds, saying the starting point out loud every single time — ‘first from the left’ — fixes more confusion than any worksheet. Skip it and children quietly assume everyone starts where they do, which is exactly the photo-line argument we began with.

Where ordinals show up in real life

The reason to bother with this is that ordinals are everywhere a child looks, so practice can be free and constant. A few contexts that make it click:

  • A race or sports day: who came first, second, third. The medal ceremony is ordinal numbers made visible.
  • A queue at the shop: ‘we are fourth in line’ is a natural, patient-making use of position.
  • Floors of a building: the flat on the third floor, the lift button for the seventh. In many Indian buildings the ground floor complicates this nicely — a good honest wrinkle to discuss when a child is ready.
  • Days and dates: the first of the month, Republic Day on the twenty-sixth, a birthday on the ninth.
  • Steps and instructions: first do this, second do that. Ordinals quietly teach sequence.

One caveat worth keeping in mind: do not push past tenth too soon. Eleventh, twelfth and the rest can wait. A Grade 1 child who is rock-solid on first to tenth, and who always states the starting end, is in far better shape than one who can recite to twentieth but points at the wrong child in a line.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz on exactly this — naming a position in a row, matching an ordinal to its word, and counting from the other end. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for written practice, the printable worksheet at the end has graded ordinal-number questions from first to tenth with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 1 Ordinal Numbers Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on first to tenth: naming positions, matching ordinals to words, and counting from the other end. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 1 ordinal numbers, first to tenth

questions.q: Five children stand in a row: Riya, Kabir, Sana, Dev, Priya. Counting from the left, who is 3rd?
questions.explanation: Count from the left: Riya is first, Kabir second, Sana third. So Sana is 3rd.

questions.q: In a race, Meera finished just after the winner. What position is Meera?
questions.explanation: The winner is first. The runner just after the winner is second.

questions.q: Which word means the same as 4th?
questions.explanation: 4th is written as the word fourth. Most ordinals after third just add th to the number.

questions.q: Six cars are parked in a line. Counting from the right, which position is the last car on the left?
questions.explanation: There are six cars. Counting from the right, the far-left car is the sixth one you reach.

questions.q: What is the correct short form for seventh?
questions.explanation: Seventh is written 7th. Only 1st, 2nd and 3rd use st, nd and rd; the rest use th.

questions.q: The shop queue has Dev first, then Aarav, then Sana, then you. What position are you?
questions.explanation: Dev is first, Aarav second, Sana third, and you are fourth in the queue.

questions.q: Which ordinal comes right after eighth?
questions.explanation: The order goes eighth, ninth, tenth. Ninth comes right after eighth.

questions.q: Riya, Kabir, Sana, Dev, Priya stand in a row. Counting from the right, what position is Kabir?
questions.explanation: From the right: Priya first, Dev second, Sana third, Kabir fourth. So Kabir is 4th from the right.

faq.q: What is the difference between cardinal and ordinal numbers?
faq.a: Cardinal numbers tell you how many — three apples, six children. Ordinal numbers tell you a position in an order — the third apple, the sixth child. Same numbers, different job.

faq.q: Which ordinal numbers should a Grade 1 child know?
faq.a: First to tenth is the right target for Grade 1, along with the short forms 1st, 2nd and 3rd. Save eleventh and beyond for later — being solid on the first ten matters more than reciting a long list.

faq.q: Why is my child confused about who is second in a line?
faq.a: Almost always because the starting end was never stated. Position changes depending on whether you count from the left or the right, so always say it out loud — second from the left, second from the right — and the confusion disappears.

faq.q: How do I explain the spellings of first, second and third?
faq.a: Those three are exceptions and sound nothing like one, two, three, so teach them as their own small set. After that, most ordinals just add th, with fifth, eighth and ninth as the tricky spellings to watch.
